title: Why a walking robot can't just switch off, and the standard being written for it
excerpt: Humanoid and legged robots fall over if their power is cut. Here is why that makes stopping them safely different, and what the draft ISO 25785-1 standard covers.

sources.title: ISO: ISO/CD 25785-1 Robotics – Safety requirements for dynamically stable industrial mobile robots – Part 1: Robots
arXiv: Toward Certified Functional Safety for Industrial Humanoid Robots – The Fail-Passive Gap and a Feasibility Study

body_html:
For most machines, the safest way to stop is to cut the power. A factory robot arm or a wheeled delivery robot simply halts where it is. Humanoid robots, four-legged robots and self-balancing wheeled robots are different: they stay upright only because their control system is constantly working to keep them balanced. Switch them off, and they can fall.

That simple fact is why international standards experts are writing a separate safety standard for these machines.

Static and dynamic stability

A robot on four wheels or a fixed base is statically stable: it stands up on its own when nothing is happening. A walking or balancing robot is dynamically stable, or has "actively controlled stability": it needs power and continuous control to stay upright. A fall is a hazard in itself, because a heavy machine toppling near a person can injure them.

The "safe state" problem

Classic machinery safety rules assume that a machine's safe state is the switched-off state. Engineers call this "fail-passive": if something goes wrong, removing power makes things safe. A research paper published on arXiv in August 2026 calls the mismatch for walking robots the "fail-passive gap". The authors write that for a legged robot, the safe state is "an actively-controlled state", such as a controlled, balanced standstill.

Industrial stop functions are usually grouped into categories. In the simplest, power is removed immediately. In another, the machine is brought to a controlled stop first and power is removed afterwards. For a balancing robot, the paper notes that an immediate power cut is exactly what it cannot safely do. A controlled stop is needed, and that stop depends on the robot's own control software still working, which makes it harder to prove reliable to the levels safety certification usually requires.

In their tests, the researchers brought a humanoid robot to a stable standstill within 0.5 to 1.3 seconds when its communication link was cut in several different ways. They are clear that this does not amount to a certified safety system.

What ISO 25785-1 will cover

The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) is developing ISO 25785-1, "Safety requirements for dynamically stable industrial mobile robots (legged, wheeled, or other forms of locomotion)". According to ISO's page:

  • It covers industrial mobile robots that need active control to stay balanced, with any number of legs or wheels, with or without arms.
  • It applies to workplaces where the public is excluded or restricted. Robots in homes and public spaces are outside its scope.
  • It addresses significant hazards during intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse.
  • Part 1 covers the robots themselves. A planned Part 2 will cover how they are integrated into workplaces.
  • Driver-controlled robots, robots that people ride or wear, and road vehicles are excluded.

The standard is still a committee draft under review by ISO's robotics committee (ISO/TC 299). It has not been published, so its final requirements could change.

What this means for people

Humanoid and legged robots are being developed and trialled for industrial work. Until a dedicated standard is final, there is no agreed international benchmark for how such a robot should stop, fall or recover near people. Homes and public spaces are not covered even by the draft.

If you work near, or are considering, a walking or balancing robot, useful questions include:

  • What does the robot do when someone presses stop: freeze, sit down, lower itself, or cut power?
  • What happens if it loses its connection or its software crashes?
  • How does it detect a fall, and can it fall in a controlled way away from people?
  • Which safety standards was it tested against, and by whom?

These questions sit behind D1 Always stoppable and D3 Physical safety. Because a remote stop depends on a working, secure connection, they also connect to D6 Secure and supported. More questions are on our questions to ask page.
